readerTitle: Want more loyal customers? First, plan how to lose them
caseNote: 가상 사례 (청소 서비스 두 곳, 레스토랑) + 일화 (Jacobi, Munger의 말)
insight: 성공하는 방법이 막막할 때는 질문을 뒤집어 '어떻게 하면 확실히 망할까'를 묻고, 그 목록에서 지금 하고 있는 일부터 멈춘다.
misconception: 좋은 결과를 얻으려면 좋은 아이디어를 더하는 데 집중해야 한다. 실패 원인을 따지는 것은 비관적이고 시간 낭비다.

sources.text: Charlie Munger, 1986 Harvard School commencement speech ("How to Guarantee a Life of Misery"), reprinted in Poor Charlie's Almanack
"Man muss immer umkehren" (invert, always invert), commonly attributed to mathematician Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi
청소 서비스와 레스토랑 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Jacobi의 "man muss immer umkehren"은 널리 인용되지만 1차 문헌 출처는 분명하지 않습니다. 카드에는 "is often credited"로 적었습니다.
Munger의 '어디서 죽을지 알면 거기 안 가겠다'는 농부 일화는 Munger가 여러 연설에서 전한 이야기입니다. 직접 인용 대신 풀어 쓰고 일화로 표시했습니다. 1986년 Harvard School 졸업 연설 연도와 제목을 게시 전 확인하세요.
청소 서비스와 레스토랑 사례에는 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다. 모든 내용은 가상입니다.

cards.title: Want more loyal customers? First, plan how to lose them
body: Two home cleaning companies in the same town had the same problem: customers kept cancelling after a few months.
One owner asked, "How do we delight our customers?" The other asked, "How would we lose a customer for sure?"
Only one of them fixed the problem.

image.label: Two cleaning vans facing opposite directions
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 같은 모양의 청소 서비스 밴 두 대가 서로 반대 방향을 보고 서 있음. 한 대 위에는 반짝이는 별 말풍선, 다른 한 대 위에는 뒤집힌 물음표 말풍선. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Customers cancel after a few months.
body: You run a home cleaning service. New customers sign up happily, then many cancel within three or four months. You have time and money for one fix this quarter.

options.text: Add small extras: a thank-you card, a fresh flower, a folded towel
options.feedback: Extras can feel nice, but they don't touch whatever is actually driving people away. You add cost and may miss the real cause.

options.text: List what would make a customer cancel for sure, then check which of those you already do
options.feedback: This points you at concrete failures you can stop. It takes honesty, because some items on the list will be your own habits.

options.text: Offer a discount for signing a 12-month contract
options.feedback: It may hold customers longer on paper, but unhappy customers locked in a contract tend to leave angry and tell others.

cards.title: The backwards list was more useful.
body: The first owner's ideas were pleasant but vague. The second owner wrote down how to guarantee a customer leaves:
list: Send a different cleaner every visit
cards.callout: She was doing three of the four. Fixing them cost less than the extras.

cards.title: Inversion: think backwards
body: **Inversion** means flipping a goal into its opposite. Instead of asking how to succeed, ask how you would fail. Then avoid those things.
Success is often hard to picture. Failure is usually easy and specific. Most people can name five ways to ruin a dinner party in seconds, and those five things are a good checklist.

image.label: An arrow flipping from 'How do we win?' to 'How would we fail?'
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 "How do we win?" 말풍선, 가운데에 둥글게 뒤집히는 화살표, 오른쪽에 "How would we fail?" 말풍선과 그 아래 체크리스트 3줄. 단순하고 따뜻한 색감.

cards.title: "Invert, always invert."
body: The phrase is often credited to the 19th-century mathematician Carl Jacobi, who solved hard problems by working them backwards.

Investor Charlie Munger made it famous in business. In a 1986 graduation speech, instead of advice on a happy life, he listed ways to **guarantee a miserable one**. He also liked to tell a story, likely embellished, about a farmer who only wanted to know where he would die, so he'd never go there.

cards.title: Flip, list, then check yourself.
body: State the goal. Flip it. List the ways to fail. Then mark which ones you are already doing. That last step is where the value is.
Inversion is not the same as a pre-mortem, which imagines one specific plan has already failed. Inversion works on any goal, even before you have a plan.
cards.softwareNote: Ask "How would we make sure a new user quits in week one?" The answers, like a confusing signup or no clear first step, often make a sharper roadmap than a list of new features.

cards.title: Avoiding failure is not the same as winning.
body: Stopping mistakes keeps customers from leaving. It doesn't always give them a reason to choose you in the first place. You still need something people want.
The failure list can also grow endless and make a team timid. Rank the items by how likely and how costly they are, and fix the top few.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant launch.
body: You run a busy restaurant. This Friday you launch a new dinner menu and want the night to win you regulars.
What's the best use of your prep time this week?

image.label: A restaurant kitchen pass with order tickets piling up
image.brief: 레스토랑 주방의 패스 카운터. 주문 티켓이 줄줄이 걸려 있고, 옆 칠판에 "How could Friday go wrong?"라는 손글씨 목록. 실제 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

options.text: Add a free welcome drink for every table
options.feedback: Guests will enjoy it, but a nice touch won't save the night if the kitchen falls behind on new dishes.

options.text: Run social ads to fill every table on Friday
options.feedback: More guests means more pressure on a menu the kitchen has never cooked at speed. You'd show the most people your roughest night.

options.text: List how Friday could be ruined, like slow new dishes, sold-out items or staff who can't describe the food, and fix those
options.feedback: You find the likely failures while there's still time to rehearse. It feels less exciting than a promotion, but it protects the first impression.

cards.title: To find the path to success, map the road to failure first.
body: When a goal feels vague, flip it. The ways to fail are usually clearer, and some of them are already happening.
**Try it today:** write one goal for this month. Then write five ways you could guarantee it fails. Circle any you're doing now.
